original_finding.evidence: Proof 3.1 says “for s\ge0, w_k^{2s}\ge1, hence the coefficient sequence is in \ell^2 and [F4] gives its unique L^2 representative.” The cited Fourier-basis result [F4] gives a representative in complex L^2. The defined completion is over real trigonometric polynomials with conjugate-symmetric coefficients; the proof does not show that the resulting complex representative is real-valued. Comparing it with its conjugate using Fourier uniqueness would close this small gap.

proposed_repair.exact_replacement:
3.1 Since $w_k^{2s}>0$, symmetric truncations to $|k|_\infty\le M$ converge in the weighted $\ell^2$ norm by convergence of the defining nonnegative series. The conjugate-symmetry condition is preserved by these cutoffs, so the completion is exactly the real weighted coefficient subspace. For $s\ge0$, $w_k^{2s}\ge1$, hence the coefficient sequence is in $\ell^2$ and [F4] gives its unique initially complex $L^2$ class. For each component $f$ of this class, complex conjugation preserves $L^2$ and the normalized coefficient convention gives
$$\widehat{\overline f}(k)=\overline{\widehat f(-k)}=\overline{a_{-k}}=a_k=\widehat f(k),$$
where $a_k$ is its coefficient coordinate. Uniqueness of Fourier synthesis in [F4] therefore gives $f=\overline f$ almost everywhere, so $\operatorname{Re}f$ is a real representative with the same coefficients. Applying this to the finitely many components gives a real $\mathbb R^N$-valued representative, unique up to equality almost everywhere by the coefficient isometry in step 2.1. For $s<0$ the construction gives only the weighted coefficient completion and makes no $L^2$ claim. [given, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
